This confirms the claim that the methods estimate radiance by reconstructing values from discrete samples using spatial blurring.

A technique to convert a long beam estimator into a short beam estimator by treating the beam length sampling as a Russian Roulette (RR) decision on the contribution [S1].

The claim is explicitly stated in the notes and elaborated upon in Section 7.3 of the source text. The text describes interpreting short beams as a Russian roulette (RR) decision on the outcome of the long-beam estimator. It provides the specific mechanism: making a zero contribution if the beam is too short, and otherwise dividing the original long beam estimator result by the RR probability (the probability that the beam length exceeds the query distance). This matches the claim exactly.

The short beam estimator is calculated as $\langle I \rangle_{\text{short}} = \langle I \rangle_{\text{long}} \frac{H(l - t)}{\Pr\{l > t\}}$, where $H$ is the Heaviside step function [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in Section 7.3 (Equation 54 and surrounding text) that a long beam estimator can be converted to a short beam estimator by making a zero contribution if the beam is too short (using the Heaviside step function H(l - t)) and dividing by the probability that the beam length l is greater than the distance t (Pr{l > t}). This matches the formula provided in the claim exactly.

A zero contribution is made whenever the beam length $l$ is less than the distance to the query point $t$; otherwise, the original long beam estimator result is divided by the RR probability $\Pr\{l > t\}$ [S1].

The claim is explicitly supported by the text in Source [S1], specifically in Section 7.3 ('PDFs of Long and Short Beams'). The text states: 'Any long beam estimator can be converted to a corresponding short beam estimator by making a zero contribution whenever the beam is too short to make the considered contribution, else by the original estimator divided by the RR probability'. This matches the claim's description of making a zero contribution when beam length $l < t$ and dividing by the RR probability otherwise.
